entities.name: Ibak Khan
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Ibak Khan, also known as Sayyid Ibrahim Khan, Ivak, or Abak, was a pivotal Shaybanid khan who ruled the Tyumen Khanate in Western Siberia during the late 15th century, dying in 1495. His strategic defeat of Ahmed Khan, the last Great Khan of the Golden Horde, in 1481 near the Ugra River, decisively ended over two centuries of Tatar dominion over Muscovite Rus', a turning point that profoundly reshaped the political landscape of Eastern Europe and paved the way for Russian sovereignty. Ibak Khan’s actions were central to the complex power struggles among the fragmented successor states of the Golden Horde, solidifying his role as a key player in the transition from Mongol suzerainty to emerging regional powers.

Emerging from the nomadic traditions of the Shaybanid branch of the Golden Horde, Ibak Khan established his authority over the Tyumen Khanate, a precursor to the later Sibir Khanate, by the 1470s. His most celebrated military achievement occurred in 1481 when, in alliance with the Nogai Horde, he ambushed and killed Ahmed Khan, who was retreating after the Great Stand on the Ugra River against Ivan III of Muscovy. This audacious strike not only eliminated a formidable rival but also effectively shattered the last vestiges of the Golden Horde's centralized power, preventing its potential resurgence and freeing Muscovy from its long-standing tributary status. Ibak Khan's rule was characterized by ongoing conflicts with other Tatar factions and the consolidation of his own nascent khanate.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Ibak Khan's decisive defeat of Ahmed Khan in 1481 definitively ended the Golden Horde's suzerainty over Muscovy, a pivotal event that paved the way for the rise of an independent Russian state and reshaped the geopolitical landscape of Eastern Europe.
